messages.body_plain:
Hi UNMARKED Google Members,

I simulated data to evaluate the performance of the n-mixture model for repeated visits and the multinomial Poisson model with removal sampling to test the utility of both models for bat ecological studies. I ran multiple scenarios – varying sample size (number of sites), number of visits, and probabilities of detection and population sizes.

I found that overall the n-mixture model overpredicted abundances for most of my simulated datasets, whereas, the removal sampling model was accurate in predicting the population size for most variations within a scenario.

I did not include covariates in either model, as I wanted to understand how both preformed without additional factors that would affect abundance estimates.

Does anyone have a possible explanation why this is happening? Or has anyone else found similar results?

Thank you all for your time,

Kathryn

messages.body_plain:
Hi Sarah

I see two possible ways how to address your 'Era' question in unmarked.
(1) Use dynamic occupancy models and then estimate the occupancy status of each site with ranef(). You can then add up the number of sites occupied at least once during each era to obtain a finite sample estimator of occupancy. Not sure about the variance though, could presumably get at it using a bootstrap. This approach allows for the fact that there will likely be colonisations and extinctions within each era
(2) Treat both eras as closed periods and fit either a static model (using occu()) to stacked data, treating era as a factor, or else, again use a dynocc model (with colext()) with just two primary periods.

Given the long period in between the eras and the relatively short duration of each era (btw, does 5 +3 add up to 8 or 9 ?), the latter would perhaps be my preferred approach.

Best regards  --- Marc

Dear Sarah,

If using occu() (i.e. you fit a static model) I would simply assume closure over the 5 and 3 years respectively. No pseudoreplication then. Assuming closure amounts then to interpret the occupancy parameter as “occupancy sometimes during the entire period over which closure is assumed”, which is 5 and 3 years. Especially given the relatively long interval between these two eras, I think this makes very much sense and is even a desirable interpretation of the occupancy parameter.

Best regards  ... Marc

messages.body_plain:
Dear Adrian,

To be honest, I feel that you have a need to get your homework done before you ask further questions on this list. It may be that I don’t fully understand your problem, and if this is the case, I apologize, but if you are asking what I believe you do then clearly, you don’t grasp the meaning of the occupancy part of an occupancy model as a simple regression model. You have something there that looks like this:

logit(psi) = alpha + beta * tree.

unmarked yields estimates of the parameters alpha and beta. The magnitude and sign of beta give you a first indication of how the relationship between tree and psi looks like. And then,  you can combine alpha and beta with a range of values of the covariate tree to produce predictions of what one expects psi to be when one varies tree.

However, this is a basic problem about regression and not something that is particular about occupancy models. You can read up on this in any introductory stats book. For the specific case of a regression model as part of an occupancy or other hierarchical model, we have lots of examples of how to form predictions in our AHM1 book.

Why p should be modeled before psi ? Well, p is usually regarded as less interesting (a “nuisance parameter”) and in models such as occupancy models (but also Cormack-Jolly-Seber survival models), people usually feel that they want to get the nuisance done with before going to the (usually) biologically more interesting parameters, such as occupancy or survival.

Best regards    --- Marc

logit(psi) = alpha + beta * tree.

For the specific case of a regression model as part of an occupancy or other hierarchical model, we have lots of examples of how to form predictions in our AHM1 book.

Hi Darryl,

I really appreciate you taking the time to answer my question.

I reread MacKenzie and Bailey (2004) and found the following statement: "By considering the contribution of each observed detection history to the test-statistic, it appears the poor fit is caused by an unusually large number of sites where the salamanders were detected on each sampling occasion. This may be due to an unmeasured site characteristic that also affects detection probabilities, or possibly caused by the species occurring at higher densities at those sites (probability of detecting at least one member of the species could be higher at sites where the species is more abundant). We suggest that this should be kept in mind when drawing conclusions about the affects of the available covariates from this analysis."

I think this is what you're referring to, yes? I do indeed appear to have the same issue with 36/87 sites having a capture history of all detections. I noticed that in the 2004 paper, in the initial salamander example you perform an all subsets analysis and use some of the same covariates (D,E,V, and S) to model both the occupancy and detection parameters. I did not do this - I stuck to the rule of site covariates (occupancy) vary by site, and visit covariates (detection) vary by visit. I included Julian date, air temperature, precipitation, and visit number (i.e., 1,2,3, or 4) as detection covariates. When comparing models with different combinations of these detection covariates (and keeping occupancy constant), Julian date emerged as the most parsimonious, therefore I used it as the detection component for all subsequent models.

On your recommendation (and on a hunch) I just tried using wetland size (i.e., "hectares") as a detection covariate under the logic that painted turtles occur with greater density in larger wetlands. It improved things a little bit, but there is still strong evidence of lack of fit (p-value = 0.044; c-hat = 1.79). Given my methods (trapping) I'm not really sure what else would be driving detection. So I suppose I still have a couple questions regarding how to proceed...

-  Should this be interpreted as general evidence of lack-of-fit for this species, and should I therefore perform QAIC for model selection? I've used BIC for all other model selection procedures for this and the other species considered to this point - would I have to change them all for ease of interpretation, or can I just do painted turtles using QAIC?

- Is it adequate to simply inflate the SEs by a factor of the c-hat and then considered the top model supported? Or should the top model simply be ignored and we conclude there is little inference on which to advance?

- Should I try modelling the detection parameter with additional site-level covariates before coming to the conclusion that there is evidence of lack of fit?

Can't thank you enough for the help. Much appreciated.

-Scott B.

messages.body_plain:
I am working with data from a camera survey conducted on a sample of wildlife openings available on a wildlife management area. The sites used for the camera survey were spaced so that an individual would be unlikely to be observed at two different sites during the survey period. Using the models generated from Unmarked on this data set, I am now trying to simulate a occupancy/density estimate for every wildlife opening across the management area. From this I hope to generate a WMA wide average of occupancy and density.

The issue I am running into is that the spacing of these openings is variable and there will be a potential for spatial auto correlation between wildlife openings. Openings that are within a certain range of other openings would have a probability of having the same individuals on each. And this probability would change depending on how close two given wildlife openings are to each other. When I average across the entire WMA, these openings are biasing my estimates by overemphasizing the areas with concentrated wildlife openings.

I have read Hines et al. 2010 and other papers discussing spatial autocorrelation in Occupancy, but they emphasize dealing with spatial autocorrelation in the initial analysis of occupancy. I haven't found much discussion on how to incorporate it into simulations, especially when there was no autocorrelation to generate the models. If anyone has any experience dealing with a problem like this or can point me in the right direction, I'd really appreciate it. Thanks!

Hi Matthew

1. Your description seems to contradict itself ("sites used for the camera survey were spaced so that an individual would be unlikely to be observed at two different sites" vs "Openings that are within a certain range of other openings would have a probability of having the same individuals"). Do you expect autocorrelation for other reasons?

2. I suggest this is best handled by simulating the entire sampling process i.e. distribute animals across the landscape according to some density model, then sample from that population using some detectors (wildlife openings?). There is another package that does this.

3. I'm not sure you should expect bias, rather there will be overdispersion (inflated precision) and poor spatial coverage.

4. Your free use of "occupancy/density" has me worried. Suggest you tie this down and think about the definition of "occupancy".

Murray
